_status: UNVERIFIED. Same discipline as spaces_v1 and setbacks_v1: every block cites a source and carries "verified": false until someone reads it against the document. These are construction dimensions rather than legal minimums for the most part, but a door narrower than the bye-law floor is still an unbuildable plan.
_frames: All figures metres, the IR-wide unit. Wall thickness is the FINISHED thickness including plaster, because that is what the drawing shows and what a room's clear internal dimension is measured against.
_zero_thickness: Stage ⑤ tiles exactly, which means its walls have no thickness — two rooms share a line. Stage ⑥ gives that line a width and takes it out of BOTH rooms, half each, so the tiling stays symmetric and no room is silently favoured. A room's clear area is therefore always smaller than the area stage ⑤ scored it at; that is the drawing being honest, not a regression.

walls.source: Practice, not code. 230 mm is one brick and 115 mm is half a brick in the 230x110x75 modular size used across south India; the Karnataka Municipalities Model Building Bye-Laws 2017 set no general wall thickness for a load-bearing dwelling of this scale.

doors._clearance: Kept between a door reveal and the end of its wall, so a door never opens flush into a return wall. Also what makes a wall too short to hold a door: anything under width + 2x clearance cannot take one.
doors.source: Practice. NBC 2016 Part 3 gives 0.75 m as the floor for a bathroom or WC door and 0.9 m for a habitable room; the 1.0 m entrance is convention, not code. Neither figure has been read first-hand — see VERIFY.md.

windows._area_fraction: The rule the bye-laws actually state: window area as a fraction of the room's FLOOR area, not a fixed opening. A 19 m² hall and a 3 m² bathroom were getting the same 1.2 m window, which satisfies neither the code nor anybody living there. 1/10th is the figure for habitable rooms.
windows._height: Openings are stored as a width along a wall, so a height is needed to get an area at all. 1.2 m is an ordinary window: 0.9 m sill to 2.1 m head, which is also the door head height, and lining them up is what a draughtsman does.
windows._min_wall: An exterior wall shorter than this gets no window rather than a token one — a 0.6 m opening in a 1.4 m wall leaves two 400 mm piers, which is not something anyone builds.
windows._widths: The clamp is what makes a second window necessary rather than optional: past 2.4 m an opening wants a mullion and is really two windows, and stage ⑥ places it as two.
windows.source: NBC 2016 Part 3 requires an aggregate openable area of not less than one-tenth of the floor area for habitable rooms, with kitchens and sanitary spaces treated separately. TRANSCRIBED FROM PRACTICE KNOWLEDGE, not read first-hand — the clause number is not recorded here because we have not seen it. The Karnataka Municipalities Model Building Bye-Laws 2017 govern in Bengaluru and may differ. See VERIFY.md.

_fixtures: Sizes are the ones an Indian sanitaryware or modular-kitchen catalogue quotes, which is what a draughtsman reaches for at concept stage. They are drawing conventions, not code: the bye-laws regulate a bathroom's AREA and ventilation, not the model of WC in it. `depth_m` is measured out from the wall the fixture backs onto and `width_m` along it.

fixtures.source: Practice. Standard catalogue sizes: a 1.5 x 2.0 m queen bed, a 600 mm modular counter depth, a 900 mm shower tray. Nothing here is a legal minimum and nothing has been read against a document.

schedules._note: Which fixtures a room gets, in the order they are placed. Order is priority: the first fixture takes the best wall, and anything that no longer fits is dropped rather than overlapped. A bathroom that can only hold a WC and a basin is a real bathroom; one with a shower drawn through the door is not.
